Components: a magic phrase (such as kitchy-kitchy-coo) while making a pinching and pulling motion with thumb and forefinger.

rolls.label: Intelligence 7+: must roll above intelligence on 3d6

system.description: Conjures an invisible key-like force that fits a lock, to open (or close) it. It works only on the simplest locks, typically those with closing pressure prongs, bolt and pins, or bolt and spring closures. Locks with tumblers or levers, and secret-combination locks, are not affected. Simple locks with complex wards against skeleton keys are affected. Components: a word or phrase about locks (tick-tock-doublelock or yah-el, etc.) while twisting the fingers as if holding a key.

Makes a noise like a door with corroded hinges slowly opening (lasting 1/3 segment), or like someone or something walking across squeaky floorboards (lasting half a segment and seeming to move up to 10 feet). Components: a low creaking in the throat, with an opening motion of the hand or fingers making a walking motion.

Creates the sound of footsteps of a human or humanoid walking, soft or fairly noisy. They can approach, move away from, follow or seem to walk alongside a person or party. They must begin within 1˝ of the caster, and can then move up to 2˝ away or come closer than 1˝. Components: softly making footstep-like sounds while pointing where they are to be.

Creates the sound of an agonized cry from a spot no more than 1˝ from the caster. Creatures within hearing get a saving throw versus spell; those who save hear nothing. Containers and doors do not block it, so the groan can seem to come from behind a door, inside a chest, etc. Components: a soft groan in the throat while pointing to where the sound should seem to come from.
The same as groan, but the sound is either a pitiful moan (high-pitched) or an eerie, haunting one (low-pitched).

Creates the sound of rattling chains, for up to 2 seconds, with the same direction and distance as groan. All creatures within 1˝ of the sound get a saving throw versus spell to see whether they hear it. Components: naming the rattling device to be imitated while shaking one hand hard.

An invisible force taps or raps on a solid object (a door, lid, floor, table, wall, pane, or whatever) once, twice or three times, according to how many fingers the caster holds out. It is a real sound, and creatures within 1˝ of it will certainly hear it if able. Components: a hollow sound of the tongue against the palate, or a softly spoken key phrase, while the finger makes a tapping motion.

An illusory sound: all creatures within 1˝ of the area hear a loud but muffled thump, as if something large had fallen from a height of a foot or so. It can seem to come from anywhere within 1˝ of the caster. A successful saving throw versus spell cancels it. Components: swallowing loudly while pointing to where the sound is to come from and thinking of the thump.

Creates a faint whistling (heard within 10’) or a loud one (heard within 30’), either sharp and normal-sounding or echoing, hollow and eerie. Components: whistling softly like the sound wanted, while looking at where it is to come from and holding two fingers near the mouth.

Sets a chosen area (a portal, a section of floor, stairs, etc.) to react to any living creature larger than a normal rat, that is, larger than about one-half cubic foot or heavier than about 3 pounds. As soon as such a creature steps on, touches or otherwise contacts the area, a loud ringing sounds for 1 segment, clearly heard within 60’ (reduce by 10’ for each door in between, by 20’ for each substantial wall).

Undead do not set it off. Invisible creatures, and creatures from other planes that are otherwise alive, do. Ethereal or astrally projected creatures do not, but flying and levitating creatures do.

Components: a tiny bell and a piece of very fine silver wire.

Creates a magical force field that acts as leather armor (AC 8). It has no effect on someone already wearing armor. On a creature whose normal armor class is better than 9 (from size, speed, skin, etc.), it improves that armor class by one step (AC 8 becomes 7, AC 7 becomes 6, and so on). It does not slow or hinder movement, adds no weight or encumbrance, and does not prevent spell casting.

It lasts until dispelled, or until the wearer has taken more than 8 points + 1 per level of the caster in total damage. For example, the wearer might take 8 points from one attack, then several turns later 1 more point; unless the caster was 2nd level or higher, the spell would end then. Until it ends, the wearer gets the full benefit of the armor class.

It does not work together with protective magic items other than a ring of protection. Component: a piece of finely cured leather blessed by a cleric.

system.aoe: 1 pint of water per level of caster
system.description:
Turns a volume of water into a volatile, flammable liquid like alcohol, and also lighter than water. Exposed to flame, fire or even a spark, it bursts into hot flames, doing 2-12 hit points of damage to each creature caught in them. It evaporates and becomes useless within 1 round, even if tightly sealed, so it must be ignited within 10 segments of its creation.

Components: a few grains of sugar and a raisin.

system.aoe: 1 sq. ft. per level of caster
system.description:
Covers an area with a slippery, greasy substance. Any creature stepping on it must save versus petrification or slip, skid and fall; a creature aware of it may be able to avoid it.

It can also coat something other than the ground: a rope, ladder rungs, a weapon handle, etc. An unattended object is always affected, but an object being held or used by a creature is affected only if that creature fails a saving throw versus spell. A single saving throw negates the effect.

Component: a bit of pork rind, butter or other greasy material.

system.aoe: 1 cu. yd. of ice or 2 cu. yds. of snow per level of caster
system.description:
Suddenly raises the temperature in the area. A 1st level magic-user can turn a cube of solid ice 1 yard on a side into water in 1 round. Twice that volume of snow can be affected: 1 cubic yard of snow melts in ½ round, or 2 cubic yards (1 yd. × 1 yd. × 2 yds.) in 1 round.

Against monsters such as white dragons, winter wolves, yeti, woolly rhinos, creatures made of para-elemental ice and the like, it does 2 points of damage per level of the caster, or 1 point per level on a successful saving throw versus spell. It is generally ineffective against other kinds of creatures.

Components: a few crystals of rock salt and a pinch of soot.

Calls a normal animal to serve the caster as a mount. It serves willingly and well, and when the spell ends it vanishes back to where it came from. Its statistics are typical for its kind. The kind depends on the caster’s level (a caster may always choose a “lower level” mount):

Caster levelMount
1st through 3rdmule or light horse
4th through 7thdraft horse or warhorse
8th through 12thcamel
13th & upelephant (and houda at 18th level)

The mount comes without riding gear, unless it is of a lower class than the caster could get: a 4th level magic-user can get a warhorse without saddle and harness, or a light horse with them.

Component: a bit of hair or dung from the kind of animal to be called.
Identical to the 1st-level cleric spell of the same name, except that no holy symbol is needed as a material component.

The recipient can run at full speed (twice normal speed) for 5-8 hours without tiring, but must then rest for the same number of hours, drink plenty and eat heartily. One more person can be affected for every 2 levels of the caster: 2 at 4th level, 3 at 6th, etc. Only humans and demi-humans in their natural forms are affected, and barbarians with that class’s special running ability are immune.

Components: an elixir of dried plum juice boiled in spring water, with the oil of 5-8 beans of a spurge (castor) plant.

system.aoe: 2 levels or hit dice per level of caster
system.description:
Lets the caster jeer and mock effectively at any creature of intelligence 2 or more; the spell gives the caster’s words and sounds real meaning to the target(s), challenging, insulting and generally enraging them. Targets that fail to save versus spell rush furiously at the caster, and every one that comes will attack if physically able, using body weapons and hand-held weapons rather than attacking from a distance. If an impassable boundary separates them (a wall of flame, a deep chasm), the spell breaks.

Only one kind of creature is affected per casting: in a mixed group of orcs and goblins, the caster could affect the orcs or the goblins, not both. The creatures nearest the caster are affected first, whatever the maximum range: a 10th-level magic-user taunting gnolls affects the nearest ten, even if he or she would rather reach the gnoll shaman at the back. Troops under a strong leader get +1 to +4 on the saving throw, at the DM’s discretion.

The magic-user inscribes his or her personal rune or mark, plus up to six smaller characters, visibly or invisibly, on stone, metal or any softer material without harming it.

Detect magic makes an invisible mark glow and become readable (though not necessarily understandable). Detect invisibility, true seeing, true sight, a gem of seeing or a robe of eyes also reveal it. Read magic reveals the maker’s intent, and erase wipes the mark away.

Components: a pinch of diamond dust (about 50 gp worth) and pigment(s) to color the mark. An invisible mark still needs the pigments, but is drawn with some sort of stylus instead of a finger.

Any rope-like object of non-living material (string, yarn, cord, line, rope, even cable) obeys the caster’s commands. It affects about 50’ of normal rope (1 inch thick) plus 5’ per level of the caster; reduce the length in proportion for thicker material, and increase it by 50% when the thickness is halved.

Commands: Coil (into a neat stack); Coil & Knot; Loop; Loop & Knot; Tie & Knot; and the reverse of each (Uncoil, etc.). The rope must be within about 1 foot of an object to act on it properly, so it usually has to be thrown nearby.

A creature caught by it can handle it as a normal object: the creature’s grip overrides the magic, and the rope breaks after 2 points of slashing damage. It cannot be used as a garrot, but can be a trip line or entangle a single opponent (as the druid spell). It gains no magical properties beyond obeying commands (cf. rope of climbing, rope of entanglement).

Prepares a garment to hold far more than normal. A finely sewn gown or robe of high-quality material (worth at least 300 gp) is made with many hand-sized pockets, at least a dozen. The spell then works in one of these ways, with no visible bulge:

  • One pocket holds 1,000 gp weight (5 cubic feet) as if it weighed only 100 gp.
  • Or 10 pockets each hold 100 gp weight (½ cubic foot each).
  • Or, in a garment with 100 or more pockets (costing at least 1,000 gp), 100 pockets each hold 10 gp weight (1/6 cubic foot each).

If the spell ends, or dispel magic is cast on the garment, while things are in the pockets, the wearer saves versus spell. On a failure, the contents pass from extra-dimensional space to astral space and are lost forever. On a success, they suddenly appear around the wearer and fall to the ground.

Components: the garment, a tiny golden needle, and a strip of fine cloth given a half-twist and fastened at the ends.

Creates a burning globe of normal fire up to 1˝ from the caster, which rolls in the direction the caster points, even uphill, at 1˝ per round. It rolls over low barriers such as walls, furniture, etc., if they are no more than 4’ tall. If the caster stops pointing, it stays where it is, burning. It sets fire to flammable things it touches. Creatures it strikes take 2-8 points of damage, and all creatures within 5’ of its center must save versus spell or take that damage; a successful save negates it. It can be put out like any normal fire of its size.

Components: a bit of tallow, a pinch of sulphur and a dusting of powdered iron.

Affects the target’s skin. Creatures with very thick or insensitive skin (such as buffalo, elephants, scaled creatures, etc.) are basically unaffected. Either of two versions can be cast from the same preparation:

Itching: the target feels an instant itch somewhere on its body. Unless it spends 5-8 segments scratching it at once, it spends the next 3 rounds squirming and twisting, at 4 worse armor class and -2 “to hit”. Spell casting is ruined during the first round of the effect, but not during the three rounds after.

Rash: the target notices nothing for 1-4 rounds, then its whole skin breaks out in faintly itching red welts. The rash lasts until cure disease or dispel magic is cast on it. It lowers comeliness by 1 point per day for four days (4 points at most), and after one week dexterity also drops by 1 point. All symptoms vanish and all statistics return to normal as soon as the rash is removed.

Component: powdered leaf of poison ivy, oak or sumac.

Apart from the differences given in the spell’s statistics, this is the same as the 2nd-level cleric spell of the same name. A target examined for only one round reveals only its ethical alignment (law/chaos).

Creates a magic “arrow” that flies to its target as if shot from the bow of a fighter of the caster’s level. It counts as a +1 weapon for hitting, and because of its acid it can harm a target even if arrows or +1 magic weapons normally could not.

  • The arrow itself does 2-5 points of damage.
  • On a hit, acid gushes out, equal to an 8-ounce acid missile (1’ diameter area, 2-8 hit points of damage, plus item saving throws; no splash).
  • For every 3 levels of the caster above the 3rd, the acid does one more round of damage: a 4th-6th level magic-user’s acid damages over two rounds, unless the target can get it neutralized.

Components: a dart, powdered rhubarb leaf and adder stomach.

system.aoe: ½ cu. ft. per level of caster
system.description:
Keeps an item fresh and whole until it is needed later in a spell. It does not preserve the potency of material such as mistletoe, holly berries and similar things that must be gathered regularly, and does not preserve the dead for later resurrection; otherwise it works. What can be preserved depends on the caster’s level:

  • Hard, fairly dry material: 2nd-4th level
  • Soft, fairly wet material: 5th-7th level
  • Semi-liquid and liquid material: 8th level & up

A container is needed only for fairly moist material. Components: a pinch of dust, a bit of resin (or amber) and a drop of brandy.

Gives immunity to cantrips cast by other magic-users, apprentices, or creatures that use cantrip magic. It protects the caster, or one item or person touched (such as a spell book or a drawer of spell components). Any cantrip cast at the protected person or item vanishes with an audible pop. It is often used by magic-users with mischievous apprentices, or who want their apprentices to clean or shine with elbow grease instead of magic. An unwilling target must be touched (a roll “to hit”) and gets a saving throw versus spell.

The target finds everything hilariously funny. The round the spell is cast it feels only a slight tingling; the next round it begins smiling, then giggling, chuckling, tittering, snickering, guffawing, and finally collapses in gales of uncontrollable hideous laughter. The laughter lasts only that single round, but the creature spends the next round getting back on its feet, and suffers −2 strength (or −2 “to hit” and damage) on the 3rd and 4th rounds after casting.

A successful save versus spell negates it, adjusted by intelligence: 3 or less, totally unaffected; 4-8, saves at −6; 9-12, at −4; 13-15, at −2; 16 or greater, normal.

Components: a small feather, a tiny wooden paddle and a minute tort. The tort is thrown at the target, the feather waved in one hand, and the paddle tapped against the caster’s own backside.

The recipient can cast spells that normally need a verbal component without making a sound, as long as each such spell is cast entirely within the vocalize spell’s duration. It is very useful when quiet is wanted, or under a silence spell. It does not overcome silence for other speech or communication (a message spell could be cast from inside magical silence, but no reply could reach the caster); it only offsets silence for casting. Any sound a spell cast this way would make is masked while the silence lasts.

Component: a bell without a clapper, or a jailbird’s tongue.

Creates a material, whip-like lash up to 1˝ from the caster, who wields it by moving his or her hand as if holding a real whip. Each turn it can both crack loudly and strike.

Against animals: the crack alone keeps normal animals at bay unless they save versus spell. An animal actually struck (a normal “to hit” roll) must save versus spell at −1 to −4 or slink away and not return for at least an hour. The whip does no actual damage. It does not affect creatures with intelligence above 3, giant animals larger than bear-size, or monsters.

Disarming: in melee, a hit means the lash has wrapped around the opponent’s weapon. The whip then saves versus crushing blow (13 or better) if the weapon is edged, or versus normal blow (6 or better) if not, with the weapon’s magic bonus as a penalty. If it succeeds, the weapon is torn from the opponent’s hand and thrown to the ground, unless the opponent makes a saving throw versus spell; the opponent then needs 1 round to recover it. The target’s magic resistance must fail before a “to hit” roll is even possible.

Component: a small bit of silk braided into a miniature whip.

rolls.label: Save penalty for an animal struck

system.aoe: 1˝ path, ½˝ per level in length
system.description:
A gentle draft of air flows from the caster in the direction he or she faces, out to the full area of effect.

  • Small flames waver and dance.
  • Larger flames and fires are fanned hotter (+1 on damage dice, if applicable).
  • Moving clouds of vapor (such as cloudkill) are held back for 1 round.
  • Fog cloud, wall of fog and similar vapors are weakened, halving their duration.
  • Stagnant air, vapors or even poisonous gases are pushed back 1˝, which also halves their duration and potency, unless something renews them.

Component: a piece of fine parchment, folded like an accordion and pinned near the bottom with a pin of ivory or silver.
Identical to the 3rd-level cleric spell of the same name, except that no holy symbol is needed as a material component.
Apart from the differences given in the spell’s statistics, this is the same as the 1st-level illusionist spell detect illusion.

system.aoe: 2 cu. ft. per level of caster
system.description:
* Duration quadrupled if used on non-living material.

The caster touches any normal, non-magical item small enough for the area of effect and shrinks it to one-twelfth of its normal size, optionally also changing the shrunken item into a cloth-like material. Only living things get a saving throw versus spell, at +4. Objects and creatures changed to cloth make later saving throws normally (as if not changed). An item returns to its normal size and material if thrown onto any solid surface, or at the original caster’s command. The spell can affect a fire and its fuel.

system.aoe: 1 cu. ft. per level of caster
system.description:
Creates certain common things. Common basic materials in raw, unworked form, such as stone, earth (soil) or wood, are easy to produce, as are other inorganic or non-living materials such as water, air, dung, straw, etc.

Simple plants (an area of grass, for example) have a base 100% chance of total failure, less 1% per level of the caster. Animal life can never be created. Worked, refined or manufactured items can never be created, nor can rough gems or precious metals. In short, the spell creates common things of a basic nature.

Lets the caster throw small globes of fire, each bursting on impact into a 1 ft. sphere, doing 1-4 points of damage to the target or setting combustibles alight (even solid planks). They are thrown missile weapons; misses are treated as grenade-like missiles. The caster can throw as many as he or she has levels, until choosing to give up the rest, or until a dispel magic succeeds against the caster.

When casting, the caster chooses one of two firing rates, and cannot switch afterwards:

  • Rapid: one missile every 2 segments. The caster points at a target on the second segment after casting and a missile flies; this repeats every 2 segments until all are gone, so the spell usually carries over into at least the next round.
  • One per round (starting with the round of casting): the caster can hold or throw missiles at will, as long as one is thrown each round. This lets the caster throw a meteor and cast another spell in the same round, as long as the other spell does not need continuing concentration (if it does, the caster involuntarily loses the remaining meteors). The benefit is great enough that the risk does not matter. If the caster loses exact count of how many missiles remain, that is a sure sign he or she has involuntarily given up the rest of the spell.

Components: nitre and sulphur formed into a bead with pine tar, and a tiny hollow tube of gold. The tube costs at least 1,000 gp to make because of its fine workmanship and magical engraving, but it lasts through many castings unless damaged by accident or abuse.

rolls.label: Damage per meteor
rolls.note: One meteor per caster level; roll each as it is thrown.

system.aoe: One page of any size up to 2 ft. square
system.description:
Changes how a page’s contents look, so it seems to be something entirely different: a map might look like a treatise on burnishing ebony walking sticks, or a spell’s text like a ledger page or even another spell. Confuse languages and explosive runes can be cast on the page, but comprehend languages will not reveal its true contents.

The caster can speak a command word to reveal the real page, read it, and return it to its secret form afterwards; saying the word twice removes the spell. Others who notice the page’s dim magic can try dispel magic, but if it fails, the page is destroyed. Short of alter reality or wish, only will-o-wisp or boggart essence reveals the true contents of a page not subjected to dispel magic.

Component: powdered herring scales.

All three forms of this spell eventually call up a deep brown, snake-like force, the sepia snake, which strikes at the nearest living creature (never the caster). It attacks as a monster with hit dice equal to the caster’s level.

If it hits, the victim is engulfed in a shimmering amber force field, frozen and immobile until the caster releases it or dispel magic does. Until then nothing can reach the victim, move the field, or affect it or the victim. The victim does not age, get hungry, sleep or regain spells, and is unaware of the surroundings.

If it misses, it vanishes in a flash of brown light with a loud noise and a 1˝ puff of dun-colored smoke that lasts 1 round.

The three forms: 1) a glowing sigil drawn in the air and pointed at the target; 2) an umber glyph marked on a surface, triggered by touching or gazing at it; 3) a small character written into some magical writing to protect it.

Components: 100 gp of powdered amber, a scale from any snake and a pinch of mushroom spores.

system.aoe: An area 1˝ wide and ½˝ high per level of caster
system.description:
Creates an invisible curtain of strong wind, enough to blow birds as large as crows upward or tear papers and similar things from unsuspecting hands (if in doubt, a saving throw versus spell decides whether the holder keeps hold). Normal insects cannot pass it. Loose material, even cloth garments, caught in it flies upward.

Components: a tiny fan and a feather of exotic origin.
Similar to the 3rd-level illusionist spell of the same name, but a magic-user counts as two levels below his actual level when trying to dispel illusion/phantasm spells cast by an illusionist.

system.aoe: 30 sq. ft. per level of caster
system.description:
Many rubbery black tentacles spring from the ground, floor or other surface (even water) in the area: one per level of the caster. Each is 10’ long, AC 4, and takes as many points of damage to destroy as the caster has levels.

Any creature within reach of a tentacle can be attacked; if several are within reach of one tentacle, roll to see which it attacks. The victim saves versus spell:

  • Success: 1-4 hit points of damage from the first contact, and that tentacle is destroyed.
  • Failure: 2-8 points of damage, and the tentacle wraps around the victim, doing 3-12 points on the second and each later round.

The tentacles have no intelligence, so they may wrap around any object (a tree, post, pillar) or keep squeezing a dead opponent. Once wrapped around something, a tentacle stays there until destroyed by some attack or until the spell ends.

Component: a piece of tentacle from a giant octopus or giant squid.

system.aoe: 30 sq. ft. per level of caster
system.description:
Creates a sturdy cottage or lodge of material common in the area (stone, timber, or at worst sod), with 30 square feet of floor per level of the caster, level, clean and dry. It looks like a normal cottage, with a sturdy door, two or more shuttered windows and a small fireplace.

Protection: it withstands winds up to 70 miles per hour. It has no heating or cooling beyond natural insulation, so it must be heated like a normal home, and extreme heat will certainly affect it and its occupants. Otherwise it is very secure: as strong as a normal stone building whatever its material, resisting flame and fire like stone, and generally impervious to normal missiles (but not those of siege machines or giants). The door and shutters are wizard locked, and the chimney is secured by an iron grate at the top and a narrow flue. All three are also protected by an alarm spell (qv). An unseen servant (qv) is also called up to serve the caster.

Furnishings: crude furniture as the caster wishes: up to 8 bunks, a trestle table and benches, up to 4 chairs or 8 stools, and a writing desk.

Components: a square chip of stone, crushed lime, a few grains of sand, a sprinkling of water and several splinters of wood, plus the components of alarm and unseen servant if those are included (string and silver wire and a small bell).

Turns a normal mirror into a scrying device like a crystal ball; see the crystal ball description on p. 141 of the DMG for how it is used. The mirror must be finely made, highly polished silver costing at least 1,000 gp. It is not harmed by the casting, but the other components are used up: the eye of a hawk, an eagle or even a roc, and nitric acid, copper and zinc (cf. the 5th-level cleric spell magic font and the 2nd-level druid spell reflecting pool).

Spells through the mirror: comprehend languages, read magic, tongues, infravision and ultravision work normally. Detect magic, detect good/evil, message and detect illusion each have a 5% chance per level of the caster of working correctly.

The target may realize it is being watched: use the base chances in the crystal ball description, plus a base 5% chance for a cavalier and 1% for a barbarian.

system.aoe: 1 ft. diameter sphere per level of caster
system.description:
A globe of shimmering force encloses the target, if it is small enough to fit inside and fails a save versus spell. It holds the target for the spell’s duration and cannot be damaged by anything except a rod of cancellation, a wand of negation, or disintegrate or dispel magic, which destroy it without harming the target. Nothing passes through it in either direction, but the target can breathe normally. The target’s struggles only move the sphere, and people outside can also move it.

Components: a hemispherical piece of diamond (or similar hard, clear gem) and a matching hemispherical piece of gum arabic.

The caster releases an ear-splitting noise in a cone from his or her mouth to a 3˝ end point. Every creature in the cone is deafened for 2-12 rounds and takes the same amount (2-12 points) of damage, unless it makes a saving throw. Any exposed brittle substance that sonic vibrations can break is shattered, such as a wall of ice. It can be used only once per day, or the caster might permanently deafen himself or herself.

Components: a drop of honey, a drop of citric acid and a small cone of bull’s or ram’s horn.

The creature becomes virtually immune to any attack by cut, blow, projectile or the like: even a sword of sharpness, a rock thrown by a giant or a snake’s strike would not affect it. Magical attacks such as fireball, magic missile, lightning bolt and so forth work normally. The first attack or attack sequence from any single opponent ends the spell, though the creature is immune to that attack or sequence. Attacks with fairly soft weapons, such as a monk’s hands or an ogrillon’s fist, do 1-2 points of damage to the attacker per attack and do not end the spell.

Components: granite and diamond dust sprinkled on the recipient’s skin.

The recipient can see in the ultraviolet spectrum. At night this means clear vision, as in daylight, out to 100 yards, and shadowy, unclear vision from 100 to about 300 yards. On a very dark night under thick clouds, ultravision is reduced by 50%. Where more than about 6 feet of earth or 3 feet of stone lie between the sky and the viewer (almost anywhere underground), the ultraviolet rays are blocked and only the dimmest vision is possible in about a 3-foot radius (better if a source of emission is nearby). Nearby light, including that shed by magic items, tends to spoil ultravision, its brightness “blinding” the eyes to dimmer areas further away.

Component: a crushed amethyst worth at least 500 gp.

Sets up a natural repulsion between the object and all living things. A creature trying to touch it is either pushed back (unable to come within 1’) or pushes the object away, depending on their relative mass: a lone halfling trying to touch an iron chest under this spell is thrown back; a dozen halflings cannot get within 1’ of it; the chest skitters away from an approaching giant-sized creature.

It cannot be cast on living things, so an attempt to cast it on clothing or possessions carried by a living creature gives that creature a saving throw.

Reverse (attraction): sets up a natural attraction between the object and all living things. A smaller creature is drawn to the object; if the creature has more mass, the object slides toward it. Once stuck to another object or creature this way, the object can only be pulled off with a successful bend bars roll.

Component (either version): a magnetized needle.

A magic-user on the Prime Material Plane forces or allows a creature from another plane to return to its proper plane (cf. the 4th-level cleric spell abjure). The caster must know the name of the creature’s type, and its given, proper or surname if it has one.

Resolution: any magic resistance is checked first. Then compare the caster’s level with the creature’s level or hit dice: if the caster’s is higher, the difference is subtracted from the creature’s saving throw; if the creature’s is higher, the difference is added to it. Exception: a creature that wants to be dismissed makes only an unmodified saving throw. Certain arcane works are said to greatly improve the chance of success. If the spell succeeds, the creature is instantly whisked away, but there is a 20% chance it goes to a plane other than its own.

Reverse (beckon): tries to bring a known, named (if applicable) creature from another plane. Success is figured the same way, but magic resistance is checked only if the creature has no known proper name. If it succeeds, the creature is instantly transported to the caster’s plane. This does not make it friendly or obedient without some further constraint, so protective measures are usually taken, and even with careful preparation the results may be unpleasant.

Neither version works on creatures native to the Prime Material Plane that travel to other planes (such as shedu), or on creatures partly descended from the Prime Material Plane (such as cambions).

Components: vary with the creature: things hateful and distasteful to it for dismissal; pleasing, desirable and rewarding things for beckon.

An attempt to force compliance or obedience from a hostile or oppositely aligned creature from a plane other than the caster’s. The verbal component must address the creature’s kind and contain as much information about it as possible. The spell works in three stages:

  • While it is read: the creature feels uneasy, and saves versus commands and non-offensive spells (including charms) at -1 (favoring compliance).
  • The next round: it grows nervous and doubtful; the adjustment becomes -2.
  • The last round: it feels a dull, all-encompassing dolor; the adjustment becomes -3.

After that the creature is no longer affected and saves without adjustment.

Danger: while the caster speaks the spell, a creature of higher intelligence can attack the caster mentally, with a 5% chance per point of greater intelligence of charming and dominating the caster, then doing with him or her as its alignment dictates. If the caster is distracted or interrupted while casting, the creature automatically charms and dominates the caster.

system.aoe: 1 cu. yd. per level of caster
system.description:
Turns material into a finished product of basically the same material: a wooden bridge from a clump of trees, a rope from a patch of hemp, clothes from flax or wool, and so forth. Magical or living things cannot be created or changed. The quality of the result matches the quality of the material. With mineral material, the area of effect is reduced by a factor of nine (1 cubic yard becomes 1 cubic foot).

Items needing high craftsmanship (jewelry, swords, glass, crystal, etc.) can only be made if the caster actually has great skill in that craft. Casting takes 1 full round per cubic yard (or foot) of material.

system.aoe: One or more creatures in a 1˝ radius
system.description:
Fascinates, confuses and then enrages one or more creatures that understand the caster’s language. The caster starts talking about some topic of interest to them. All saving throws for this spell are modified by the target’s intelligence: 2 or lower, not affected; 3-7, -1; 8-10, normal; 11-14, +1; 15 or higher, +2.

Fascination: those who fail their save versus spell immediately start conversing with the caster, agreeing or disagreeing, most politely. As long as the caster keeps talking with them and no one attacks them, they ignore everything else around them, spending all their time talking and arguing.

Confusion: if the spell goes on for more than 3 rounds, each subject saves again. Those who fail wander off in confusion for 3-12 rounds, keeping away from the caster. Those who save stay fascinated, and must save again in the 4th, 5th and 6th rounds (or as long as the caster keeps it up) to avoid confusion.

Rage: if it goes on for more than 6 rounds, each subject must save versus spell or fly into a rage for 2-5 rounds: at itself if it is the only subject (attacking itself with normal “to hit” chances), or otherwise falling on the nearest other subject with intent to kill. Those who save realize they have been tricked and collapse on the ground lamenting their foolishness for 1-4 rounds, unless attacked or otherwise disturbed.

If the caster is attacked or distracted while keeping the spell going, he or she is still protected, since the subjects do not notice. The caster can leave at any time after casting, and the subjects carry on for 1 full round as if he or she were still there; in that case no further saving throws for confusion or rage apply. The spell is entirely verbal.

The caster contacts one creature he or she knows, whose name and appearance are well known to the caster. If it is on another plane, there is a 5% chance per plane of separation that the sending does not arrive (10% at two planes away). The caster can send one word per level, not counting articles (a, an and the). The message is understood even by a creature of intelligence as low as 1 (animal intelligence), but it need not act on it in any way.

Component: two tiny cylinders, each open at one end, connected by a short piece of copper wire.

A single stroke of lightning ¼˝ wide leaps from the caster’s fingertips to a primary target within range (which depends on the caster’s level). Unlike lightning bolt, it strikes a target, not an area. The primary target takes 1d6 per level of the caster, or one-half on a successful saving throw versus spell.

Arcing: the bolt then jumps to the nearest other object, animal, vegetable or mineral, and from that to the object nearest it, and so on, possibly bouncing back and forth between two (presumably stationary or immobilized) objects or cycling among three or more. Between equally near targets it chooses metal first, then the one with the most fluid, otherwise at random. It strikes as many “links” (including the primary target) as the caster has levels: a 12th-level magic-user’s chain lightning hits the primary target and then 11 others (not necessarily different ones).

Secondary targets: each object struck after the first gets a saving throw versus spell, if applicable; if it succeeds, the stroke jumps past it to the next nearest target and it takes no damage. The chain continues until it has struck the full number of objects (counting targets that fail their save or get none, such as non-magical objects), until it fades out, or until it hits something that grounds it. Direction never matters, but distance does: no single arc can be longer than the range limit, and if the next jump would be longer, the stroke fades away. A tree or a substantial piece of conductive metal (such as the connected iron bars of a large cell or cage) grounds it.

Damage: each target after the primary one takes one d6 less: if the primary target took 12d6, the next takes 11d6, then 10d6, 9d6, 8d6, 7d6, and so on down to 1d6. A saving throw for half damage applies on each strike, separate from the save to see whether the lightning hits a secondary target at all. The caster can be hit by his or her own spell.

Components: a bit of fur; an amber, glass or crystal rod; and one silver pin per level of the caster.

rolls.label: Damage to the primary target (one die less for each later target)

system.description:
The magic-user places another spell on himself or herself that takes effect when a situation stated during casting occurs. Contingency and its “companion” spell are cast together (the 1-turn casting time covers both).

The companion spell must affect the caster’s own person (feather fall, levitation, fly, statue, feign death, etc.) and be of a level no higher than one-third of the caster’s level (rounded down), and no higher than 6th: 4th level at most for a caster of 12th, 13th or 14th level; 5th level at 15th, 16th or 17th; 6th level at 18th and beyond. Only one contingency can be active at a time; casting a second cancels the first (if still active).

The condition must be clear, though it can be fairly general. For example, with airy water as the companion, the contingency might trigger whenever the caster is plunged into or engulfed by water or similar liquid; or a feather fall might trigger whenever the caster falls more than 2’. The companion spell then takes effect instantly. Complex, complicated and/or convoluted conditions are likely to make the whole thing simply fail when called on.

Components (besides the companion spell’s): 100 gp of quicksilver, an elephant ivory statuette of the caster, and an eyelash from an ogre magi, ki-rin or similar spell-using creature. The statuette is not destroyed (though it may suffer wear and tear), and must be carried by the caster for the contingency to work.

A dangerous attempt to lure a powerful creature from another plane into a specially prepared trap, where it is held until it agrees to perform one service in return for its freedom. The creature’s type, and its specific, proper or given name if it has one, must be known and used.

The lure: the creature becomes aware of a gate-like opening on its plane. It makes a special saving throw to see whether it recognizes it as a trap: it must roll its intelligence or less on 3d6, modified by the difference between its intelligence and the caster’s (subtracted from the roll if the creature’s is higher, added if the caster’s is higher). If it saves, it ignores the opening and the spell fails. If not, it steps through and is ensnared.

Protection: the ensnared creature is free to harm its captor, so the caster uses a magic circle (for creatures from the upper planes or the Astral Plane), a thaumaturgic triangle (Ethereal, Elemental or Concordant Opposition planes) or a pentagram (lower and infernal planes). Even so, the creature may break free and take vengeance:

  • Base chance: 20% for a hand-drawn design; 10% for an inlaid or carved one, and that only the first time (showing whether the work was done properly).
  • Modifier: compare the caster’s intelligence plus level with the creature’s intelligence plus level or hit dice. Subtract the difference from the chance if the caster’s total is higher; add it if the creature’s is higher.
  • Careful preparation: a hand-drawn design inscribed slowly with specially prepared pigments (1,000 gp per turn) reduces the chance by 1% per turn so spent. An inlaid or inscribed design can be brought to 0% by inlaying various metals, minerals, etc., taking at least one full month and adding at least 50,000 gp to the cost. Either can bring the base chance to 0%, but the intelligence and level/hit dice modifier still applies afterwards, and no preparation removes that risk.

Any break in the lines, or blurring of the glyphs, runes and sigils, spoils the barrier and lets the creature go free automatically; even a straw dropped across a circle’s lines destroys its power. Fortunately the creature inside cannot so much as put a straw on any part of the design, since the barrier’s magic absolutely prevents it.

Bargaining: the creature can be held as long as the caster dares (remember the danger of something breaking the design!). The caster offers bribes, promises or threats to get one service. The DM rates what the caster said from 0 to 6, and subtracts this from the creature’s intelligence; if the creature then rolls equal to or less than this adjusted intelligence, it refuses. New offers can be made, or the old ones repeated, 24 hours later, when confinement has lowered its intelligence by 1 point. This continues until it agrees, breaks free, or is released by some riddance spell. Certain other spells can of course be used to force a captive into submission.

When the service is done, the creature need only tell the caster to be instantly returned to where it came from. It may seek revenge (cf. efreeti, aerial servant and invisible stalker). It will never agree to impossible or unreasonable commands.

The caster meets the target’s gaze and speaks a single word. Each casting gives one of four effects, chosen by the caster, and the spell then ends:

  • Charm: the target becomes absolutely loyal and docile toward the charmer, even at risk to itself; otherwise as charm person or charm monster. A successful saving throw versus spell negates it.
  • Fear: the target acts as if struck by a fear spell, unless it saves versus spell.
  • Sicken: sudden nausea and sickness sweep over the target. Its ability scores (strength, intelligence, etc.) are halved by pain and fever (creatures without ability scores are not affected), it moves at half speed, and must rest half of each turn to move at all. A save versus spell negates it; otherwise the victim loses one real point of constitution per day until it dies at zero. Dispel magic or heal ends it, as do alter reality, limited wish and wish, but not cure disease. All non-human, non-demi-human and non-humanoid creatures save at +4 against this effect.
  • Sleep: the target falls into a comatose slumber unless it saves versus spell. Creatures normally affected by the 1st-level spell sleep save at −2. Undead are immune. Sleepers must be shaken or otherwise shocked awake.

Instantly recalls one spell of 1st to 5th level that the magic-user memorized and actually cast within the past 24 hours, exactly as if it had never been cast. It can be cast normally on any later round. If it needs material components, it cannot be used until they are available.
Identical to the 6th-level druid spell of the same name, except for the differences given in the spell’s statistics; the magic-user does not need mistletoe.

system.aoe: 2 levels/HD of creature(s) per level of caster
system.description:
Forces creatures from another plane back to their own home, instantly. A banished creature cannot return without some special summoning or way out of its own plane. Several creatures can be banished if the caster is powerful enough (has enough levels) and all are within range. The caster must name the type of creature(s), give its true and proper name as well, and call on powers opposed to it. The creature’s magic resistance must be overcome for the spell to work at all.

Components and saving throw: the components are substances harmful, hateful and/or opposed to the creature’s nature. Each one used gives the creature −2 on its save versus spell: iron, holy water, sunstone and a sprig of rosemary used against a demon make its save −8 (four substances times 2). Special items, such as hair from a ki-rin’s tail or couatl feathers, can count for −3 or −4 each. In contrast, a devil’s scale, a titan’s hair, or mistletoe blessed by a druid might count for only −1 against a demon.

If the creature saves, the caster is stung by a backlash of energy, taking 2-12 points of damage and being stunned for 2-12 segments.

If the powers called on are directly and actively opposed to the creature(s), or favorably and actively concerned with the caster’s interests, they can add from −1 (least concerned) to −6 (most concerned) to the components’ effect, as the referee judges.

rolls.label: Backlash to the caster if the creature saves

system.description:
Creates a cube of force, but unlike the magic item cube of force, its walls are not solid: they are bands of force with ½’ gaps between, a true cage. Creatures in the area are trapped unless they can fit through the gaps, and all spells and breath weapons pass through the gaps freely. A creature with magic resistance can use it in one attempt to pass through the walls; if it fails, the creature is caged. Either way, all other creatures in the area stay trapped unless their own magic resistance lets them escape. Unlike the cube of force, it can only be removed by dispel magic or by the spell ending.

Forcecube: with special preparation when memorizing, the spell can instead create a forcecube, one-eighth the area (a cube 1˝ on a side), which works like a cube of force in every way except for the differences between a cast spell and a device, including how it can be defeated.

Casting either version needs no material component, but memorizing it does: the magic-user powders a diamond worth at least 1,000 gp and traces the outline of the cage or cube with the dust. When the study is finished the dust is tossed into the air and disappears.

system.aoe: 300 sq. ft. per level of caster
system.description:
Conjures an extra-dimensional dwelling that can only be entered at one point in space on the plane where it was cast. Observers see only a faint shimmering in the air there, about 4’ wide and 8’ high. The caster controls entry; the portal closes and becomes invisible behind him when he enters, and he can reopen it from his side at will.

Inside is a magnificent foyer and many rooms beyond, furnished, with enough food to serve a nine-course banquet to as many dozens of people as the caster has levels, and a staff of near-transparent, liveried, obedient servants to wait on everyone. The air is clean, fresh and warm. Conditions outside do not affect it, and conditions inside do not pass outside.

The food: resting inside is normal, but the food is not. It seems excellent and filling while inside, but its effects vanish the moment one leaves, and ravenous hunger strikes unless real food was eaten. For each imaginary meal eaten, a person must spend 1 hour sitting and eating normal food. Otherwise he or she loses 1 point of strength per such meal; eating as described restores it, but only if done within 6 hours, or the loss is permanent.

Components: a miniature portal carved from ivory, a small piece of polished marble and a tiny silver spoon, all utterly destroyed by the casting.

(This spell has been used together with a normal portal, and with illusion magic. There is evidence that the design and interior can be changed to suit the caster.)

Hides the affected object(s) from detection and location spells, and makes them invisible to every form of sight or seeing, so it can mask a secret door, a treasure vault, or whatever. It does not stop discovery by touch, or by devices such as a robe of eyes or a gem of seeing. An unwilling creature able to resist gets a normal saving throw versus spell. Living creatures (and even undead) affected become comatose, held in suspended animation until the spell ends or is dispelled.

Components: a basilisk eyelash, gum arabic and a dram of whitewash.

Like teleport, the caster travels with the weight allowed by that spell, but to any known place on his or her home plane with no chance of error. The caster can also travel to other planes, but any such plane counts at best as “Studied carefully”, and only if the caster has actually been there and carefully examined an area to use as a destination. The teleport table is used for other planes, according to how well the caster knows the destination. (Exception: see the 9th-level magic-user spell succor, described hereafter.) The caster can do nothing else in the round of arrival.

Forces submission and obedience from a captive creature from another plane, from which a service is being demanded (see also dolor and ensnarement). The first words of the spell link the caster to the creature held in a magic circle, thaumaturgic triangle or pentagram (the creature must first fail any magic resistance check). The caster then reads on through the specially prepared writing, and each round the captive feels worse: twinges in rounds 1-2, shooting pains in rounds 3-4, aches and then cramps in rounds 5-6.

Saving throws: each round a creature that refuses to serve makes a straight saving throw versus spell, at −1 in the first round, −2 in the second, −3 the third, −4 the fourth, −6 the fifth and −8 the sixth. A failure means it agrees to the caster’s demands. There is no penalty after round 8 in any case.

If it breaks loose: the creature suffers −1 on initiative for every 2 rounds the spell has run, up to −4 at round 8. It is also −1 to hit and −1 per die of damage after 3 rounds of the spell, worsening by −1 per round to −4 at round 6, then improving again to −1 at round 9.

Any intelligent creature with low morals will probably submit once it understands what is being done to it, though it will feel nothing but immense hatred for the caster. It will carry out the service to the letter, as with all such bargains, but will certainly seek whatever revenge it can.

Preparation and risks: the incantation must include either the secret name of the creature’s type or its given name, and the caster must identify himself or herself, which creates the link. But for every point of intelligence the creature has above the caster’s, there is a 1% chance that it gains control, drags the caster into its prison, and carries him or her off to its own plane to whatever fate awaits. If the caster is interrupted or distracted while reading, the chance is 5% per point of the creature’s intelligence.

Component: the “specially prepared writing” (a scroll), whose special inks cost at least 1,000 gp per hit die of the creature.

Gives the caster great power over any living thing whose true name, generic or individual, he or she knows. Most true names are unknown (even to their owners), since common names are not true and secret names; they are found through hard work, spying, and extensive use of legend lore and sagecraft (at the most difficult levels).

Casting: the caster calls out the true name and recites verse about the subject’s nature and/or history (3 segments), then, still in verse (preferably rhyming or near-rhyming), describes the result wanted. If the caster is interrupted at any point, the spell fails and is lost. The possible results:

Multiple suggestion: 1 to 4 suggestions (see suggestion), each taking a verse of 1 segment; 4 suggestions take 7 segments in all, including the opening.

Weakness and surrender: each segment of verse costs the subject 1 point of strength (−1 to hit and damage, −1 movement rate), and with each point lost it must save versus paralyzation or meekly surrender. Strength returns 2-8 rounds after the recitation stops, and with it the will to resist.

Polymorph: as polymorph any object, with no system shock roll. The verses needed (1 segment each) depend on how radical the change is, and the reverse of each case is the same:

ChangeVerses
mineral to animal10
mineral to vegetable9
vegetable to animal8
monster to normal7
monster to monster6
other to human5
animal to animal4
vegetable to vegetable3
mineral to mineral2

For cases not listed, the DM uses the closest one. The subject eventually returns to its natural form: duration is 6 turns per level of the caster, minus 1 turn per verse needed. It thinks and behaves exactly like a real thing of its new type, but keeps its original hit points.

Transport: the subject is teleported without error or otherwise moved elsewhere. Verses needed:

DestinationVerses
same plane, 100 mile range4
same plane, 500 mile range5
same plane, 2,000 mile range6
one plane/world removed7
two planes/worlds removed8

The subject is automatically changed so it can physically survive the normal conditions where it is sent. Willing subjects get no saving throw, even if they have magic resistance.

A very dangerous spell that lets the intended target of a spell turn it back on its caster, so its range, duration, area and saving throw depend on the situation and the spell volleyed. For example, a magic-user protected by volley is targeted by power word kill: the power word bounces back to its caster, who must save versus spell or suffer it. If the original caster saves, the spell flies back at the original target, who must then save or be affected; if that save succeeds, it goes back to its originator, and so on, until one of them fails to save or the spell runs out of power.

The whole spell is volleyed: a lightning bolt that would begin 10 feet in front of the volleying magic-user is returned in full, leaving others in the volleyer’s party unharmed. Each exchange takes a single second.

Running out: a spell loses its power after as many exchanges as its level, each volley (but not the original casting) counting as half an exchange. A 1st-level spell is cast, volleyed once, (perhaps) volleyed back, and then dissipates; a 2nd-level spell goes through four volleys (two full exchanges) before it is exhausted; and so on.

Component: a bit of bent willow or other flexible wood, criss-crossed with specially prepared strands of gut.

Captures a creature from the lower planes that is already held by some kind of restraining diagram. The duration depends on the form of binding, the level of the caster(s) and how long the spell is actually chanted.

Components: continuous chanting read from the scroll or book page; gestures suited to the form of binding; and materials such as miniature chains of special metal (iron for demonkind, silver for diabolical creatures, nickel for the minions of Hades, etc.), the rarest sleep-inducing herbs, a very large diamond or corundum (1,000 gp value per hit die of the subject), and a vellum picture or carved statuette of the subject.

Saving throw: none if the caster’s level (or casters’ combined levels) is at least twice the subject’s hit dice. Otherwise the subject saves versus spell, modified by the form of binding and the ratio of levels to hit dice. For this, the principal caster’s level is increased by one-third of the level of each assisting magic-user of 9th or higher level, and by one level for each assistant of 4th to 8th level. No more than six other magic-users can assist.

Forms of binding (with saving throw modifiers):

  • Chaining (normal save): restraints that create an antipathy affecting all creatures who approach the subject, except the caster. Lasts up to one year per level of the caster(s). The subject stays inside the diagram (as also with slumber and bound slumber).
  • Slumber (+1): a comatose sleep lasting up to one year per level of the caster(s).
  • Bound slumber (+2): chaining and slumber combined, lasting up to one month per level of the caster(s).
  • Hedged prison (+3): the subject is moved to or brought inside a confined area it cannot leave by any means until freed. Lasts until the magical hedge is somehow broken.
  • Metamorphosis (+4): the subject changes into some non-corporeal form, except for its head or face. Permanent until some prescribed act frees it.
  • Minimus containment (+5): the subject is shrunk to one inch tall or less and held in the hedged prison of a gem or similar object.

The subject of minimus containment, metamorphosis or hedged prison radiates a very faint aura of magic. If the subject was first weakened by dolor, it saves at −1 more; by torment, −2; by both in succession, −4. A successful save lets it burst its bonds and do as it pleases.

Renewal: the first three forms can be renewed, since the subject has no chance to break them; after one year it gets a normal saving throw versus spell, and whenever that succeeds, the binding breaks and it is free. (If anything has weakened the chaining or slumber, such as attempts to contact or magically touch the subject, a normal saving throw applies to the renewal.)

Essentially the same as sending, except that the message can contain a suggestion. If the subject fails its saving throw versus spell, it does its best to carry out the suggestion. If the message is practically impossible or makes no sense given the subject’s circumstances when it arrives, the message is understood, but no saving throw is needed and the suggestion has no effect.

Components: a pair of cylinders, each open at one end, connected by a thin piece of copper wire, and some small part of the subject (a hair, a bit of nail, etc.).

system.aoe: 1' diameter sphere per level of caster
system.description:
Exactly the same as the 4th-level magic-user spell Resilient Sphere, except that the inside of the globe is nearly weightless: anything inside weighs only 1/16 of its normal weight. Once the sphere has enclosed its subject(s), the caster can lift a subject of up to 5,000 pounds telekinetically, controlling the sphere up to 1˝ per level away. Even if more than 5,000 pounds is enclosed, it weighs only 1/16 as much, so the globe can be rolled without great effort. Because of the reduced weight, fast movement or falling inside the sphere is fairly harmless to what it holds, though it can be disastrous if the globe vanishes while high above a hard surface.

Components: those of the resilient sphere plus a pair of small bar magnets.

system.aoe: One creature or one object of 1 cu. ˝ per level of caster
system.description:
The caster must chant for 4 segments without interruption. The target is then rooted to the spot unless it saves: versus spell for a creature, or versus disintegration for an object with magical properties. Non-magical items get no saving throw. (“Magical properties” include those of magic items listed in the DMG, items enchanted or otherwise of magical origin, and items with protection-type spells or permanent magic on them.) If the save fails, the target also takes on the density of the surface it stands on.

The caster can stop here, leaving the target as it is; the spell then fades in 4 turns and the target returns to normal. If the caster continues, the target slowly sinks into the ground: one-quarter of its height on the 5th segment, another quarter on the 6th, another on the 7th, and on the 8th segment it is completely sunk.

This entombment puts a living target into a state like stasis without otherwise harming it. Living or not, the target lies undamaged in the material it sank into, its top as far below the surface as it is tall: a 6’ tall target is 6’ down, a 60’ tall one has its top 60’ below ground. If the ground around it is somehow removed, the spell breaks and it returns to normal (but does not rise up). Dig, transmute rock to mud and freedom (the reverse of imprisonment) do not harm it, and often help recover it.

Detect magic cast over the area shows a faint, undefinable dweomer even if the target is beyond detection range; if it is within range, the dweomer is identified as enchantment-alteration magic.

system.aoe: 2 cu. ft. per level of caster
system.description:
Turns metal, from soft gold to hard adamantite, into a substance as brittle and fragile as crystal: a sword, metal shield, metal armor, or even an iron golem becomes delicate, glass-like material easily shattered by any forceful blow. Only a wish can reverse it; dispel magic cannot.

The caster must touch the item (a hit, as in combat, if it is being worn or wielded or is a monster). Only one metal item is affected: a suit of armor being worn could be changed, but not the wearer’s shield too, or vice versa.

Saving throw: each item gets a percentage chance to save equal to 5% per point of magical bonus or protection: a +1/+3 sword 10% (the average of its two bonuses); +5 magic armor 25%; an iron golem 15% (since only +3 or better magic weapons hit it). Metal artifacts and relics are 95% likely to be unaffected.

An affected item that is not protected at once is shattered and permanently destroyed by a normal blow from a metal tool or any heavy weapon, including a staff.

Opens a channel between the caster’s plane and the Negative Material Plane, with the caster as the conductor. When he or she touches any living creature (a hit if in melee), the victim loses two energy levels (as if struck by a spectre). A monster permanently loses two hit dice, both for hit points and attack ability. A character permanently loses levels, hit dice, hit points and abilities (until regained by adventuring, if applicable).

Casting: preparation takes three segments; the material component (essence of spectre or vampire dust) is then cast forth, and on touching the victim the caster speaks the trigger word and the spell takes effect instantly.

There is always a 5% (1 in 20) chance that the caster also loses one energy level as the victim loses two. Humans or humanoids reduced to zero energy level by this spell become juju zombies.

All magic and magic items within the spell’s radius (3˝ of the caster), except those on or being touched by the caster, are disjoined. Spells being cast are separated into their individual components (usually spoiling them, as dispel magic does). Permanent and enchanted items must save (versus spell if actually cast on a creature, otherwise versus dispel magic) or become normal items. So all potions, scrolls, rings, rods et al, miscellaneous magic items, artifacts and relics, arms and armor, swords and miscellaneous weapons in range can lose all their magic. Even artifacts and relics can be affected, but with only a 1% chance per level of the caster.

Destroying artifacts is dangerous: it is 95% likely to attract the attention of some powerful being interested in or connected with the device, and if an artifact is destroyed, the caster must save versus spell at −4 or permanently lose all spell casting ability.

Essentially the same as the 7th-level cleric spell of the same name. The magic-user’s version teleports without error the person who breaks the object and speaks the command word. With the reverse, the archmage is likewise brought to that person, but unlike the cleric spell (qv), the summoned archmage has no choice but to answer, which makes this version very rare. Each plane in between has a 1% cumulative chance of causing the permanent loss of the person or caster involved.

Component: gem material worth at least 5,000 gp (faceted or not). It can only be enchanted once per month (usually on a clear night of full moon), when it is “set” for the type of succor and its destination (either where the spell is cast or an area well known to the mage).

Creates globes of pastel light of any color (cf. the magic-user cantrip bluelight): one globe 1 foot across, or two of 6 inches, three of 4 inches, or four of 3 inches. Each lights a radius of five times its diameter (a 1-foot globe lights 5 feet around it; a 3-inch globe only 15 inches). They last as long as the caster concentrates, floating near or resting on the caster as he or she wishes, within 1˝, and can be moved in any direction. Their light casts no reflections beyond 1˝ and cannot be seen beyond 3˝. Pale blue or pink light does not affect infravision or ultravision; other colors do. Components: naming the color and number of globes, then a magic word (noma, mazda, etc.), while directing them with one or more fingers.

Weakens a light source, or makes the air itself less filled with light. It can affect about 6 torches, a medium-sized fire (such as a fireplace or campfire), 72 candles, or even a light or continual light spell, within 1˝ of the caster. For one full round they give at best half their normal light: torches burn like candles, candles barely glow, a fire lights like a torch, and light spells dim to half brightness. Components: a magic phrase (such as bee-row-nout or rhee-oh-stat) and a downward motion of one hand.

The air in an area within 1˝ of the caster turns cloudy, as if with smoke or floating dust, for a single round. A target screened by it is 5% harder to hit: missiles fired at it are at −1 “to hit”, and it saves at +1 against spells (or gets a saving throw where it normally would not, though only a 5% chance). Hiding in shadows is 5% more effective inside it. Weather such as a good breeze or rain destroys it, and gust of wind disperses it at once. Components: humming a tune while passing the hands in front of the body.

Changes the face of the caster, or of another chosen human, demi-human or humanoid, by illusion: ears, hair, head shape, facial features and every other aspect of appearance. It can only be detected by a viewer who looks very closely, or one who can detect illusion and does so. Lasts 3-6 rounds. Components: touching the face, thinking of the features wanted, and speaking a word describing them.

Covers an area with an illusory scene so it looks like something else. The area must be fairly flat and featureless, and the mirage must show a real place that exists at the time and that the caster has actually seen. A saving throw versus spell applies. It lasts as long as the caster concentrates, but each round there is a 5% cumulative chance it wavers and shows its true nature. Touching it, dispel illusion or dispel magic ends it at once. Components: a word or two describing the mirage and a single pass of the hand; after that it is maintained by concentration alone.

Creates illusory sound of any kind the caster wishes, but indistinct and confusing: a murmur as of many voices behind a thick door or far away, a rushing like wings and wind together, shuffling and scraping as of many people moving things or walking slowly some distance off, etc. The sound fills a 1˝ radius, and every creature in it gets a saving throw; those who succeed do not hear it. Components: pointing at the area and softly imitating the sounds wanted.

Creates a band of pastel colors exactly like a rainbow, 30 feet long and 1 foot wide, which the caster can arch into a bow, leave as a ribbon, twist and turn, etc. One end must be within 1˝ of the caster when it is cast. Its colors glow softly and can be seen even in total (normal) darkness. If it is not to move, the caster can leave; to move it, the caster must control it by gesture and stay within 1˝. It lasts 1 round. Creatures that fail to save versus spell gaze at it for 1-4 segments, or 2-5 if it is kept moving. Components: a name of power (garland, pegee-lee, etc.) spoken while the fingers of both hands form a pyramid.

Virtually the same as phantasmal force in most ways, but the illusion is two-dimensional. Anyone viewing it from more than 45° off its horizontal or vertical viewing axis sees at once that it is an illusion, and it is invisible from the side or rear. Touch, dispel illusion or dispel magic ends it; otherwise it lasts as long as the caster concentrates. Components: a phrase describing the illusion while making a circular motion with a closed hand.

Creates a small globe of shifting color in the illusionist’s hand, which can be thrown at any opponent within 3˝ (its longest range) with no barriers in between. It is magical, so even creatures normally hit only by +5, +4, etc. weapons are affected if it hits, though magic resistance does apply. To hit: + 3 at 1˝ or closer, +2 from over 1˝ to 2˝, +1 from over 2˝ to 3˝. If it misses, it dissipates harmlessly.

Its color decides its effect. Low-level illusionists are limited in which colors they can make, but can always choose a color below their level:

Minimum levelColorDamageSpecial power
1stPearly1-4light: as a light spell, lasting 1 round/level of the caster; a target that fails to save versus spell is blinded for that time
2ndRuby1-6heat: melts up to 1 cubic yard of ice; a target that fails to save versus spell loses 1 point of strength and 1 of dexterity (or -1 “to hit” and AC) for 1 round after being hit
3rdFlame1-8fire: sets alight all combustibles within 1’ of the target, which takes 2 more points of fire damage unless it saves versus spell (or is protected from fire by magic or nature)
4thAmber1-10blindness: for 5-8 rounds unless the target saves versus spell (cure blindness or dispel magic ends it)
5thEmerald1-12stinking cloud: a magical stinking cloud of 5’ radius around the target; it must save versus poison or be helpless, and is helpless in any case until it leaves the vapors (cf. stinking cloud)
6thTurquoise2-16magnetism: electrical damage; ferrous metal worn by the target is magnetized for 3-12 rounds unless it saves versus spell. Magnetized metal sticks fast to other magnetized metal, and non-magnetized iron items cling until pulled free
7thSapphire2-8paralysis: for 5-20 rounds unless the target saves versus paralyzation
10thAmethyst(slow)petrification: turned to stone unless it saves versus petrification; even if it saves, it is slowed for 2-8 rounds (cf. slow)
12thAshen(paralysis)death: dies unless it saves versus death magic; even if it saves, it is paralyzed for 2-5 rounds

Component: a gem of the right color, or a clear crystal one (such as a diamond), worth as little as 50 gold pieces as long as the color is right.

Creates a quasi-real suit of plate mail on the subject, giving real protection unless an opponent actively disbelieves it (saves versus spell), or it is hit by dispel illusion, dispel magic or a wand of negation. Until then it protects as plate mail (AC 3, and armor type 3 as well).

It absorbs 1 point of damage per level of the caster from blows that would hit armor class 3. When it has absorbed as many points as the caster has levels, it vanishes, and any remaining and further damage goes to the wearer. It also gives +1 on saving throws against all attacks that magic armor would modify in the same way.

It does not affect the wearer’s movement or spell casting, cannot be harmed by a rust monster (which may encourage disbelief), and does not work together with any other magical protection. Component: a small plate of mithral (10 gp value), which disappears when the spell is cast.
The same as the 1st level magic-user spell read magic, except that it works only on spells usable and used by illusionists, and on other writings in illusionist magic script by illusionists.

system.aoe: One creature within 1˝ of the illusionist
system.description: Plays on natural fears so the target sees the caster as someone or something hostile (the illusionist does not know what). The illusionist simply advances menacingly, and unless the target saves versus spell, it turns and flees as directly away as it can (as a wand of fear, but without dropping what it carries). The caster does not pursue, but a phantasm from the creature’s own mind does. Each round after the first, the target gets another saving throw at a cumulative +1 per round, until it saves and the spell breaks. It only works on creatures of intelligence 1 or more.

Like change self, but the change is quasi-real: size can change by up to 50%. If the new form has wings, the illusionist can actually fly, but only at one-quarter the speed of a real creature of that kind, and two Maneuverability Classes worse (to a minimum of “E”). If it has gills, he can breathe underwater while the spell lasts. Changing into a larger creature does not give extra attacks or damage unless the illusionist is used to that form.

An illusion around the caster makes him or her, in the target’s eyes, a trusted and/or desired companion, winning its love, friendship and/or obedience. Unless the target saves versus spell, it follows the illusionist wherever possible without undue risk to its life and safety.

Requests: if they can talk, it obeys each request as long as a 3d6 roll does not exceed the illusionist’s comeliness. Requests clearly against its interests add +1 to the roll; more dangerous and unreasonable ones add +2 to +6. When a roll exceeds comeliness, the spell shatters, and the target is certainly filled with rage and hate.

Animals: normal creatures of animal intelligence stay fascinated only 1-4 days. If the illusionist has treated it well, cared for it and fed it, there is a 2% chance per point of the illusionist’s comeliness that it chooses to stay a friend and follow; otherwise when the spell ends it attacks (if not cared for) or leaves (if cared for). Non-intelligent creatures are not affected (cf. charm person).

rolls.label: Request check (3d6 at or under comeliness)

system.description: Apart from the differences given in the spell’s statistics, this is essentially the same as the 4th-level magic-user spell of the same name. Highly intelligent creatures may also be able to detect invisible creatures with ultravision, natural or magical. Component (illusionist version): powdered essence of carrots.

Sends a message or a sound effect. It travels as many tens of feet underground, or miles above ground, as the caster has levels: a 3rd-level illusionist could send it 30’ in a dungeon or three miles outdoors. It is as gentle and unnoticed as a zephyr until it reaches its destination, where it swirls and stays for two segments, delivering its whisper-quiet message (up to 12 words) or other sounds (up to 12 seconds), or simply seeming a faint, rustling stir of the air. It then fades away, as it also does if the target is out of range, if more than two hours pass, or if it is dispelled.

The caster can set its speed anywhere from 1˝ to 20˝ per round. As with magic mouth, no spells can be cast through it.

The illusionist takes on the alignment aura of any other creature within 3˝ (which must be of better than animal intelligence) in place of his or her own; the creature keeps its own alignment. Know alignment, detect good and detect evil reveal only the aura taken on. The creature whose aura is copied radiates magic, but the illusionist radiates magic only to that creature. Used with change self or alter self, it completely hides the illusionist’s real class, so he or she seems to be whatever class chosen, since a saving throw (versus spell) applies only to the aura transfer.

Creates a quasi-real, horse-like creature that can be ridden only by the illusionist, or by someone the illusionist makes it specifically for. All have black heads and bodies, gray manes and tails, milky eyes, and smoke-colored, insubstantial hooves that make no sound. They do not fight, and normal animals shun them, so only monstrous ones attack. A steed is dispelled after taking more than 12 points of damage.

It moves up to 4˝ per level of the caster. It seems to have a saddle, bit and bridle, but cannot carry saddlebags and the like, only its rider and what he or she carries. It gains powers with the caster’s level:

  • 8th level: crosses sandy, muddy or even swampy ground without difficulty.
  • 10th level: crosses water as if it were firm, dry ground.
  • 12th level: travels through the air as if it were solid ground, so chasms and the like can be crossed without a bridge (but it cannot casually take off and fly).
  • 14th level: performs as if it were a pegasus.

Creates a wind that cannot be seen or felt, but still blows light objects along, flutters curtains or drapes, flaps loose clothing (capes, cloaks, mantles), fans fires, and moves clouds of gas (wall of fog, fog cloud, cloudkill, etc.). It moves the way the illusionist points, its path growing 1˝ longer each round and its effects lasting along the whole path. It could, for example, move several sailing ships, though the first one reached would move the farthest.

The illusionist and all his or her gear become insubstantial. He or she can be hit only by +1 or better magic weapons, or by creatures able to affect those struck only by magic weapons. Most undead ignore the caster, taking him or her for a wraith or spectre, though a lich or “special” undead may save versus spell at -4 to recognize the spell. The caster can pass through small holes, narrow openings or even cracks with everything worn or held. No attacks are possible in wraithform, except against creatures on the Ethereal Plane, where attacks both ways are normal. Only dispel illusion or dispel magic can force the caster back to normal; the caster can return at will, which ends the spell.

Components: a bit of gauze and a wisp of smoke.
Essentially identical to the 3rd-level cleric spell of the same name, except that the illusionist casts it as if two levels lower: a 9th-level illusionist casts it as 7th level.

Creates a glowing band of pastel, rainbow-hued patterns with the same effect as hypnotic pattern. Once cast, the illusionist need only gesture in a direction and the pattern drifts slowly that way at 3˝ per round. It lasts 1-3 rounds without further attention, and all creatures affected (up to 24 levels or hit dice) follow the moving lights. If it leads them into danger (through flame, off a cliff), they get a second saving throw. If their view of the lights is completely blocked (by an obscurement spell, for instance), the spell ends.

Components: a crystal prism and a piece of phosphor.

Creates fog much like a wall of fog, but only a very strong wind can move it, and gust of wind has no effect. A creature moving through it advances only 1’ per 1˝ of its normal movement rate per round. A fireball, flame strike or wall of fire burns it away in a single round.

Components: a pinch of dried, powdered peas mixed with powdered animal hoof.

Makes an area look vacant, neglected and unused, with dust on the floor, cobwebs, dirt, or anything else typical of a long-abandoned place.
